title: Beyond “Denial”: Understanding and Responding to Help-Refusal in Dementia
content: Delayed or refused help-seeking is a common and consequential feature of dementia. Families often report that a relative with suspected or diagnosed dementia declines assessment, treatment, or support, leaving caregivers uncertain how to act. Refusal is frequently interpreted as stubbornness or denial, which can strain relationships and delay care. This article focuses on the refusal of the person living with dementia to seek or accept help, whether that is a first assessment or later assistance with every day and personal care, and treats denial by relatives as a contributing influence rather than the central problem. This narrative review synthesises published literature on why people living with dementia may refuse or delay help and proposes a practical, ethically grounded framework to guide family members and informal caregivers in encouraging professional assessment and in responding to refusal of care. The review draws on published systematic reviews, a scoping review, a meta-ethnography, a realist synthesis and selected assessment and primary-care literature; it did not involve a new database search, and review-level figures are attributed to the reviews that reported them. Four interacting explanations recur in the literature: (1) anosognosia, a neurologically based lack of awareness that differs from psychological denial; (2) stigma, fear, and fear of losing independence; (3) relational, communication and contextual factors, including trust and safety, how and by whom help is offered, pain, and the care environment; and (4) system barriers such as delayed recognition and fragmented pathways. A further distinction runs through the paper: denial implies an interpretation of what a person understands or accepts, whereas refusal is an observable response whose meaning must be established. Evidence for interventions that reduce refusal is strongest for music during personal care and modified bathing methods, with some support for positive communication and person-centred approaches, though quality is generally low and few studies involve family caregivers in community settings. Help-refusal should be understood as a symptom and a relational challenge rather than a character flaw, and as something to understand rather than merely to manage. This article proposes a staged, non-coercive framework (Understand, Check, Frame, Partner, Plan, Escalate, Sustain) that keeps professional assessment central, protects dignity and autonomy, and supports caregiver well-being. The framework is a conceptual synthesis and has not been empirically tested. A plain-language guide for families is provided in Appendix A.
